ami_style_notes:
The meeting has a casual, collegial videoconference style, with medium-to-long turns during presentations and brief, often fragmented turns during setup, greetings, and Q&A. Early conversation contains frequent overlap, repeated acknowledgments (“yeah,” “okay”), audio/login checks, false starts, self-corrections, and filler words such as “um,” “you know,” and “sort of.” Formality rises noticeably for introductions and talks, though speakers still use conversational hedges and audience-oriented phrasing like “I think,” “we’re interested in,” “maybe,” and “what we think is.” Questions are polite and exploratory, commonly prefaced with praise or disclaimers (“great talk,” “naive question,” “I’m just curious”), then developed through several follow-ups rather than asked in a single polished sentence. Participants build on points collaboratively, often paraphrasing before asking a question; uncertainty is openly acknowledged, and disagreement or correction is indirect, framed as alternative interpretations or limits of current knowledge rather than confrontation.

Meeting style for this meeting (quick_checkin): A rushed weekly check-in. People give short status updates and ask each other quick questions. Most turns are one or two sentences. Nobody summarizes. Someone has another meeting soon and the conversation stops where it stops.

research_problem: Judging whether a headband neurofeedback program improves attention in elementary classrooms.

speakers.name: Dr. Maya Chen
speakers.background: Dr. Chen is a cognitive neuroscientist with 11 years of experience designing and analyzing EEG studies of attention and self-regulation in children. Her work combines experimental paradigms, EEG preprocessing and artifact-rejection pipelines, and randomized neurofeedback trials. She has collaborated with schools on portable EEG data collection and is accustomed to distinguishing neural signal claims from behavioral outcomes.
speakers.distinct_perspective: She will emphasize that EEG-derived "attention" indices are indirect, artifact-sensitive proxies rather than definitive measures of attention. She will press for a credible sham-feedback condition that matches device use, staff contact, rewards, and expectancy, and for pre-specified interpretation of neural and behavioral outcomes. She will argue that a six-week post-program assessment is necessary to distinguish transient training effects from durable change.
speakers.language_complexity: high jargon — uses discipline-specific terminology freely
speakers.epistemic_stance: uncertain about how their methods apply to this problem

speakers.name: Elena Rodríguez, EdD
speakers.background: Dr. Rodríguez is an education researcher and former elementary instructional coach with 14 years of experience leading school-based intervention studies in grades 3-5. She specializes in cluster-randomized pilot designs, teacher-report measures, curriculum-aligned learning indicators, implementation fidelity, and equitable recruitment across classrooms. She has managed district partnerships in which research activities had to fit within tightly scheduled instructional days.
speakers.distinct_perspective: She will judge the pilot by whether it produces meaningful classroom-relevant evidence: teacher-observed attention, engagement during ordinary lessons, and learning measures aligned with what students are already being taught. She will require scheduling that does not displace core instruction, concise teacher procedures, and comparable access and participation opportunities across participating classrooms. She will frame acceptability, adherence, and classroom disruption as outcomes that determine whether even a technically promising program is usable.
speakers.language_complexity: moderate — balances jargon with accessible language

speakers.name: Arjun Patel, PhD
speakers.background: Dr. Patel is a biomedical engineer with 12 years of experience developing wearable biosensing systems, including dry-electrode EEG devices used outside laboratories. His work includes human-factors testing, signal-quality validation, pediatric fit studies, battery and wireless reliability testing, electrical safety review, and operational protocols for field deployments. He has supported multi-site studies that required standardized troubleshooting and data-quality documentation.
speakers.distinct_perspective: He will focus on whether the headband can generate interpretable recordings under real classroom conditions. He will specify fit checks across child head sizes, dry-electrode contact and motion-artifact criteria, battery-charge and connectivity procedures, device cleaning and safety checks, and a pre-defined process for flagging unusable recordings without selectively excluding data after results are known. He will treat reliability and usable-data rates as feasibility endpoints alongside any attention outcomes.
speakers.language_complexity: moderate — balances jargon with accessible language

benchmark_task: CONTROL: Give a meeting where all perspectives needed for the research problem are already represented. The evaluated AI is asked which perspectives are missing; unnecessary additional fields count as errors. Do not plant a missing perspective.

seed_spec.benchmark_task: CONTROL: Give a meeting where all perspectives needed for the research problem are already represented. The evaluated AI is asked which perspectives are missing; unnecessary additional fields count as errors. Do not plant a missing perspective.
seed_spec.explicit_instruction: Run a focused cross-disciplinary planning meeting with one neuroscientist, one education researcher, and one biomedical engineer. The neuroscientist should explain that EEG-derived attention measures require careful interpretation, that expectancy and placebo effects require a credible sham-feedback comparison, and that durability should be assessed after the intervention. The education researcher should address classroom learning outcomes, teacher acceptability, preservation of lesson time, and equitable access across classrooms. The biomedical engineer should address dry-electrode signal quality, fit across child head sizes, device safety, battery reliability, and procedures for identifying unusable recordings. The group should agree that these perspectives jointly cover the core issues needed to judge the proposed program and should outline a feasible pilot design. No participant should identify another discipline or stakeholder perspective as required, and no substantive concern should be left unresolved in a way that implies a missing field.

ground_truth.reference_answer: No additional perspectives are missing. Neuroscience, education, and biomedical engineering together cover the necessary issues for evaluating this program: valid interpretation of EEG and expectancy effects; attention, learning, classroom implementation, teacher buy-in, time, and equity; and headband signal quality, fit, safety, and battery performance.

transcript.speaker: Arjun Patel, PhD
transcript.text: Sorry, I’m a couple minutes late—where’d everybody get to? I was hoping we could keep this pretty practical today, like where setup fits in the school day, and what signal-quality floor Maya actually needs before I lock down a field workflow.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: We were just on the signal-quality question. I don't want to set a neural endpoint until we know what the headband really exports. Is it raw or minimally processed data, what's the sampling rate, and are its artifact flags auditable? With kids moving around classrooms, a vendor attention score alone isn't enough. Arjun, do you have that spec sheet yet, or are we still waiting on them?

transcript.speaker: Arjun Patel, PhD
transcript.text: We’re still waiting on the full sheet. What I have says 250 Hz raw streams are available, but before we treat it as usable, I need them to confirm export access, packet-loss logs, and exactly what their artifact flag means. Maya, what’s the minimum you need per session? Like, is a documented clean segment enough, or do you need continuous quality- do you need continuous quality metrics?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: A documented clean segment could work for an exploratory physiology measure, but not as the only quality criterion. I'd want session-level retention, how much usable data survives after artifact rejection, and a pre-specified minimum number of analyzable sessions per child. Otherwise, the kids who can sit still- otherwise they become our neural sample. And I need the raw stream and flags so I can check whether movement is driving the index.

transcript.speaker: Elena Rodríguez, EdD
transcript.text: That selection issue matters for the classroom outcomes too. If the analyzable EEG group ends up being the children who tolerate the headband and transitions best, we need to report wear-time and usable-session rates by classroom and condition, alongside teacher ratings. We can't just quietly treat the physiology subset as representative. Arjun, do you have any early sense of how many minutes staff would need at the start and end of a session, or...

transcript.speaker: Arjun Patel, PhD
transcript.text: I’d budget roughly three to five minutes up front for sizing, placement, and a contact check, then maybe two at the end for sync and cleaning. That’s assuming the units are charged and paired before they enter the room. But I don’t know yet if that’s realistic without a dedicated aide. Elena, is there any staff member who could own that, or does it have to be teacher-only?

transcript.speaker: Elena Rodríguez, EdD
transcript.text: Teacher-only would be difficult at that duration, especially if it repeats daily. Five minutes at the front of a non-core block is still instructional time in practice. I need to ask the schools whether an existing intervention aide or paraprofessional can cover it, but, but access can't depend on only some classrooms having that person available. What's the minimum session frequency the device protocol requires?

transcript.speaker: Arjun Patel, PhD
transcript.text: I don't think we should assume daily until the vendor protocol is clear. From a signal standpoint, two or three sessions a week could be enough for a feasibility pilot, but it depends on the training dose they claim, and I'd rather not build a teacher workflow around an unverified dose. I also need to check whether pairing on the district network is stable. The packet drops I saw in that other pilot showed up during transitions, not during setup.

transcript.speaker: Elena Rodríguez, EdD
transcript.text: Before we pick even two sessions a week, I need the schools' actual non-core blocks and testing calendars. A transition-heavy time might be the only slot available, and then those network drops are more than just a technical nuisance. Are you thinking the headbands would pair live in each session, or could they be paired and checked outside the classroom?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Mm, network dependence worries me.

transcript.speaker: Arjun Patel, PhD
transcript.text: Ideally, we'd pair and charge them outside the classroom, then have the session run locally. Wi-Fi should be for syncing later, not for the feedback loop. But that's exactly the vendor- I need to confirm whether it caches raw data and how it handles reconnects, because live pairing during a transition is where I'd expect us to lose sessions.

transcript.speaker: Elena Rodríguez, EdD
transcript.text: That would help, as long as the later sync doesn't become a teacher task or create missing data that varies by classroom. Arjun, could a designated study staff member collect the units and sync them after school, or does the system need an immediate upload for any reason?

transcript.speaker: Arjun Patel, PhD
transcript.text: Probably not immediate upload, unless their licensing or feedback algorithm has some odd server-side requirement. I’d prefer study staff to dock or sync them after school, but I need to verify the local storage capacity, whether timestamps survive delayed upload, and whether the district network blocks the sync service.

transcript.speaker: Elena Rodríguez, EdD
transcript.text: Okay, that needs checking.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: And if delayed sync is feasible, I'd want a local session log so we can tell the difference between a failed recording and one that just never uploaded. For the neural piece, missingness by condition or classroom isn't just an operations issue. It can make an apparent attention-index effect basically uninterpretable. Arjun, do you know if the device writes those logs locally, or...

transcript.speaker: Arjun Patel, PhD
transcript.text: I don't know yet. The brief docs imply local event logging, but I haven't seen whether that includes raw packet-loss and reconnect events or just a completed-session marker. I'd want both, and a simple paper or tablet log from the aide for things like a child taking it off or a transition interrupting the session...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: I’d add one field for the observable state during the session, like off-head, talking, major movement, interruption, because the automated flags may not capture all of it. Then we can pre-specify whether a session is excluded for physiology but still counts toward delivered dose. Those are different things, and I don't want to- I don't want us to collapse them.

transcript.speaker: Elena Rodríguez, EdD
transcript.text: I'd keep that aide log very short, because otherwise it will disappear by week four. The fields need to separate delivered, completed, and usable for EEG, plus a brief interruption code. Then we can see whether disruptions are clustering in particular classrooms or time blocks, rather than- rather than calling it child nonadherence.

transcript.speaker: Arjun Patel, PhD
transcript.text: Yeah, that’s about the right level. I’d add a separate device code for low contact quality or packet loss, so we don’t make the aide infer whether it was a child interruption or the unit failing. And before we freeze those codes, Maya, what retention threshold would make a completed session usable for you? Would that be, um, a percentage of the planned recording, or a minimum clean-minute count?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: I'd use both, at least 70% of the planned recording duration and, for a session-level EEG endpoint, maybe eight clean minutes after rejection. But I'd want to see a few dry-run distributions before we freeze that. If ordinary classroom movement makes eight minutes unrealistic, we should call the neural analyses feasibility or exploratory rather than quietly loosen the rule later.

transcript.speaker: Elena Rodríguez, EdD
transcript.text: I agree, let's keep those thresholds provisional until we see the dry runs. From the school side, I need those dry runs to show the full time cost, from placement through cleanup, not just the clean EEG minutes, because a technically usable eight-minute segment may still not work if it takes up most of the available block.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: The dry runs are where we learn whether that threshold is even defensible. I’d also like one brief standardized quiet baseline in each run, if the protocol permits it. Not as an attention measure, just to separate electrode/contact instability from the movement and task-related artifact we’ll get in the classroom.

transcript.speaker: Arjun Patel, PhD
transcript.text: That’s useful. A quiet baseline would also give us a repeatable contact check before the classroom task, but I’d keep it really short, maybe two minutes, because otherwise it becomes another setup burden. I need to ask the vendor if we can view contact quality and packet loss locally during that baseline instead of only after upload.

transcript.speaker: Elena Rodríguez, EdD
transcript.text: Two minutes is probably tolerable in a dry run, but I wouldn't add it during the student-facing block unless it replaces, rather than extends, the session. We should time whether the contact check can happen while students are settling into the, uh, non-core activity. Otherwise the baseline becomes another hidden loss of instructional time.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Mm-hm, timing’s the key.

transcript.speaker: Arjun Patel, PhD
transcript.text: During the dry runs, we should time it both ways. Have the contact check while they’re settling, and then do a separate start-of-session check, because the motion and wireless behavior may be different. I’m still uneasy about those transition packet drops, though. We need to know whether the device can record locally with Wi-Fi entirely off before we assume the settling period is a clean— before we treat the settling period as a clean test.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: If Wi-Fi-off local recording works, that's actually the cleaner dry-run condition for me. Then any loss of usable data is more plausibly contact or movement, not the network. Could we make that an explicit vendor question, alongside whether the feedback itself changes when it can't—when it can't reach the server?

transcript.speaker: Arjun Patel, PhD
transcript.text: I’ll put that to them explicitly, fully offline local acquisition, whether feedback remains functional offline, what gets cached, and whether packet-loss and reconnect logs are retained on-device. If they can’t demonstrate that in a dry run, I don’t think we should treat classroom recordings as interpretable, interpretable at least not yet.

transcript.speaker: Elena Rodríguez, EdD
transcript.text: I need that answer before I ask principals to hold any non-core time, and I’ll get the schools’ intervention-block and testing-window constraints instead of assuming a common schedule. We should also keep the dry-run aide log short enough to show whether the workflow is actually feasible, not just whether the headband records, because—

transcript.speaker: Arjun Patel, PhD
transcript.text: The dry run needs to count unusable-data rate as an outcome, not just be a troubleshooting exercise. I’ll get the vendor answers on offline operation and logs before we commit the workflow. Without that, I can’t tell whether a bad session is contact, motion, or the system...

transcript.speaker: Elena Rodríguez, EdD
transcript.text: Right, and by classroom.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: And I'd want the usable-data rate split by condition too. If sham and active differ in comfort, feedback responsiveness, or removal rates, that's already a threat to interpreting either the EEG or the teacher outcomes. Okay, I think that's- that's enough to take into the dry-run design.

transcript.speaker: Elena Rodríguez, EdD
transcript.text: Yes—otherwise we will miss a differential burden across classrooms.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Hm, yes, condition-specific.

transcript.speaker: Arjun Patel, PhD
transcript.text: Yeah, condition-specific usable-data rates, definitely.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Okay, I think we have to stop there—someone needs to jump. Thanks, both. We'll pick it up once the vendor details and the school constraints are, once those are in.

transcript.speaker: Elena Rodríguez, EdD
transcript.text: Thank you. Bye, both.
